strengths: The crucifixion case combines attestation, ordinary lethality, medical judgment, and survivor implausibility into the debate’s clearest and least controversial historical premise.
Licona anchors bodily continuity in direct Pauline grammar, Romans, and Philippians rather than relying only on later gospel physicality.
His synthesis connects death, tomb, appearances, adverse witnesses, and movement formation within one explanatory proposal that directly answers the motion.

blunders.text: The best-explanation claim declares natural theories failures before comparably measuring their probabilities, independence assumptions, and combined explanatory reach.
Religious significance risks circularly increasing the miracle prior unless divine intention is independently established rather than inferred from the disputed event.
Closing replies overstate Carrier’s account as synchronized identical hallucination and underaddress source dependence, selective disclosure, and ordinary literary development.

strengths: Carrier presses the earliest-source question through Paul’s omissions, embodiment contrasts, vocabulary, grammar, and relevant Jewish conceptual parallels here.

finalArgument.thesis: Resurrection is the strongest historical explanation when supported facts jointly resist the best specified natural alternatives.
premises: Jesus’s death is supported by converging testimony, crucifixion lethality, and the weakness of proposed survival scenarios.
Early sources indicate followers and adverse witnesses sincerely interpreted experiences as appearances of the risen Jesus.
Bodily resurrection language, Jerusalem proclamation, and hostile explanations collectively make an absent body historically relevant despite disputes.
Paul’s grammar and transformation language plausibly preserve bodily continuity rather than replacement by an unrelated heavenly person.
A successful rival must explain death, absence, appearances, and movement formation without multiplying unsupported mechanisms for each datum.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, if these strands remain substantially independent after criticism, resurrection merits preference as the most comprehensive historical explanation available.

newArguments.title: Convergence without duplication
newArguments.text: The resurrection case strengthens when each strand bears a different explanatory load. Crucifixion evidence establishes death; appearance traditions establish sincere postmortem conviction; tomb traditions address bodily absence; Pauline continuity constrains what earliest resurrection meant. No strand proves resurrection, and dependence must be discounted. Yet a rival must explain why distinct data types converge on one temporally concentrated change in belief and practice. If natural proposals require separate speculative mechanisms for the corpse, followers, Paul, James, and rapid proclamation, their familiarity may conceal greater total complexity than one extraordinary causal hypothesis.

newArguments.title: Adverse-witness discrimination
newArguments.text: Paul matters because prior opposition helps discriminate among explanations. Grief may fit bereaved disciples; expectation may fit committed followers; fraud may fit strategic insiders. Those mechanisms fit a persecutor less naturally unless evidence supports guilt, attraction, exhaustion, or prior sympathy. This argument should not exaggerate James’s hostility or treat sincerity as accuracy. It should ask which theory predicts conviction across importantly different prior attitudes with the fewest tailored additions. Resurrection gains comparative force only if this cross-group pattern is securely sourced and the proposed natural mechanisms remain independently unsupported under scrutiny.

newArguments.title: Intentional-event priors
newArguments.text: Rare events should not be assessed only by frequency when a competing explanation includes purposeful agency. A coded message can be improbable under randomness yet expected under an informed sender. Religious context could similarly increase resurrection’s probability if independent evidence supports divine action connected with Jesus’s mission. This cannot allow theology to assume its conclusion: intention and context require support separate from the event. The disciplined comparison asks whether Jesus’s claims, actions, and predicted vindication supply genuine prior information, then measures natural and supernatural hypotheses by the same explanatory standards.

finalArgument.thesis: Natural visionary and literary development is preferable unless surviving sources overcome dependence, ordinary mechanisms, and extraordinary-event priors.
premises: Paul is earliest and describes revelation, spiritual embodiment, and transformation in language contested by later physical narratives.
The empty tomb lacks the independent contemporary corroboration normally needed for a historically unnecessary and remarkable claim.
Grief, expectation, suggestion, memory convergence, and conversion visions are independently established kinds of human experience.
Later narratives add increasingly tangible, apologetically useful details that ordinary literary and sectarian development can plausibly generate.
Universal saving intention appears difficult to reconcile with brief selective appearances mediated through ancient human testimony.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, absent stronger independent evidence for bodily continuity and the empty tomb, visionary and literary processes remain the better-supported explanation.

newArguments.title: Evidence-dependence correction
newArguments.text: Apparent convergence can disappear when reports inherit the same tradition. Later narratives, hostile replies preserved by Christians, and retrospective martyrdom claims may look independent while sharing apologetic ancestry. Historical comparison should weight causal independence, not merely count sources. Begin with Paul, identify his actual commitments, then add only evidence whose transmission route is sufficiently distinct. If the empty tomb, tangible appearances, guards, and theft controversy cannot survive that correction, resurrection loses much cumulative force. The natural account needs fewer coincidences because literary dependence itself predicts repeated and increasingly concrete claims.

newArguments.title: Prediction before accommodation
newArguments.text: A strong natural theory should make risky predictions instead of accommodating every datum afterward. Visionary origins predict early revelatory language, sincere conviction without public repeatability, disagreement about embodiment, and later pressure toward tangible verification. Literary development predicts useful additions answering recognizable objections. These expectations can be compared with Paul and the gospel sequence without presuming every difference is invention. Resurrection, meanwhile, needs a specified divine intention to predict who sees Jesus, why appearances stop, and why evidence remains narrow. Without those specifications, supernatural flexibility may reduce explanatory precision under scrutiny.

newArguments.title: Selective disclosure likelihood
newArguments.text: Evidence distribution matters independently of whether resurrection is metaphysically possible. If a compassionate deity intends universal informed acceptance, broad and repeated disclosure seems more expected than appearances to a small ancient circle followed by disputed testimony. Natural religious origins regularly begin locally, spread through committed witnesses, and accumulate interpretive detail. The argument remains conditional because divine purposes might include freedom, trust, or historical mediation. Those replies nevertheless need independent grounding rather than invention to fit silence. Selective disclosure therefore asks which hypothesis predicted this geographic and temporal informational pattern before observing it.
